newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippines makes defector feel at home.
newsitem.headline: Philippines makes defector feel at home.

text.p: Top North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop is under heavy guard in a safe place, eats Korean dishes prepared by a specially hired cook and spends his time watching cable TV, senior Philippine military officers said on Saturday.

They said they had not detected the presence of any Pyongyang hitmen who might try to kill Hwang and that two North Korean agents who slipped into the Philipines several years ago were now married to Filipinos and leading quiet lives.
The two former agents, a man and a woman, entered the country using Nepalese passports, the officers said.
"But we are on the lookout," one officer said, asking not to be identified. He said about 20 military agents were keeping guard over Hwang.
Hwang is not allowed to see any visitors but occasionally chats with his cook and doctor, the officers said.
"He is in good condition .... He is staying in one place. His safety is paramount," Major General Benjamin Libarnes, intelligence chief of the Armed Forces of the Philippines, told reporters.
Libarnes said a cook who specialises in Korean dishes had been hired to provide for the defector's culinary needs.
But he refused to disclose the exact whereabouts of Pyongyang's top ideologue, who defected to the South Korean mission in Beijing on February 12 and was whisked off to the Philippines on Tuesday.
A special presidential task force has kept Hwang in a secret hideaway since his arrival in the Philippines.
Asked how long the defector would stay, Libarnes said: "Maybe less than a month."
President Fidel Ramos said last Wednesday that the Philipines had agreed to offer temporary shelter to Hwang but stressed that his stay would be "as short as possible."
Ramos has refused to give details on the whereabouts of the 73-year old Hwang, saying his safety was "of paramount importance."

Hwang's Philippine detour is seen as a compromise in the standoff between Pyongyang and Seoul over his fate. It allows North Korea to save face by not having Hwang go directly to bitter rival South Korea, where he is expected to receive political asylum.
Since Hwang's arrival, rumours have circulated about possible threats to his life.

Military officers earlier said Hwang was flown to the northern mountain resort of Baguio after his arrival at the Clark special economic zone -- formerly the U.S. Clark air base -- 80 km (50 miles) north of Manila.
A defence official said he believed Hwang was being kept at the military intelligence compound in Manila's Camp Aguinaldo.
Libarnes said Hwang was staying in a "private facility" and not in any American or South Korean establishment.
He said neither the United States Central Intelligence Agency nor any South Korean or Chinese military personnel were involved in the operations to secure Hwang's safety in the Philippines.
Asked how difficult a task it was to protect Hwang, Libarnes said: "It's peanuts."

Three days after Hwang fled to Seoul's mission in Beijing, a prominent North Korean defector was fatally shot near Seoul in an attack seen as retaliation for Hwang's defection. The victim, Li Il-nam, was a nephew of the former wife of North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
